claims.text: A liquid-precursor synthesis process can produce nanoscale single-phase ZrB2 powder.
The liquid-precursor route can be applied to ZrB2 without introducing foreign secondary phases.
The liquid-precursor route can lower the preparation or sintering temperature of single-phase ZrB2 to 1200–1800 °C and below 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 requires processing above 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 typically has relatively coarse grains and inherent porosity.
Porosity in conventionally prepared ZrB2 promotes structural degradation, hole formation, and eventual failure during exposure to aggressive liquid plating baths.
Nanoscale ZrB2 grains promote enhanced diffusion and densification.
Enhanced densification from nanoscale grains minimizes the size and connectivity of pores.
Liquid-precursor synthesis creates a highly reactive, ultrafine precursor.
The highly reactive, ultrafine precursor enables both ZrB2 phase formation and densification at a significantly lower temperature than conventional processing.
Reduced grain size improves grain-boundary diffusion.
Improved grain-boundary diffusion suppresses holes and defects that would otherwise coalesce during prolonged liquid-plating-bath exposure.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 will be more densely consolidated and have lower porosity than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 will retain better microstructural and mechanical integrity after long-duration plating-bath exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
A cited liquid-precursor study synthesized a nano-dual-phase powder with ultrafine grains at 1200 °C.
The cited study synthesized several single-phase high-entropy diboride powders at 1800 °C with average grain sizes of 340–570 nm.

The cited liquid-precursor method was not applicable to all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for single-phase high-entropy boride formation when the size-difference factor exceeded 3.9%.
Direct adaptation of the high-entropy-powder process to pure ZrB2 and scale-up to fully dense components remain uncertain.
